synthesis_provenance.first_pass_synthesis_verbatim:
I’m digging into AI agents today, and the annoying part is that “agent” can mean almost anything.

A chatbot that gives you one answer? Not really the interesting bit.

I mean a system that can make decisions, pick tools, read documents, search for information, write things down, call APIs, and keep going through a multi-step task.

Basically: AI that can do something instead of just confidently explaining how it would do it.

Which is exciting.

And also how you end up watching a tiny digital employee misunderstand its objective with incredible determination.

The part I’m researching is what actually changes when you give an AI access to tools, memory, and an environment it can affect.

Does it stay useful? Does it get confused? Does it remember what it did five minutes ago?

Well… now I want to build a small one and find out.

synthesis_provenance.corrective_pass_synthesis_verbatim:
I’m researching AI agents, and the annoying part is that the word “agent” gets used for basically anything with a chat box and a confident attitude.

But an agent is more than one response. It can make decisions, choose tools, search for information, read documents, write information, call APIs, handle multi-step tasks, keep state, and react when something changes around it.

Which is where this gets interesting.

A language model can tell you it has a plan. An agent can potentially go do parts of the plan. That does not mean it will do them well. It can misunderstand the objective, lose context, pick the wrong tool, or produce an answer that sounds extremely convincing and is still completely wrong.

I found my old workshop-agent notes again—the smaller experiment from before I gave it more context and it started making decisions about my projects.

So now I’m staring at the question I probably should have asked first: what does this thing actually need to know, remember, and be allowed to touch before it becomes useful instead of just… enthusiastic?

Because giving an AI tools is fun.

Giving it the wrong tools is how you create a very polite problem.

Tell me: what would you make an agent try first?
